summary:
South Carolina stands under the United States federal framework on travel documents, and that framework carries the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passport applications are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed those passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Visa screening adds its own exposure: since February 2025 the State Department has barred trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging applicants with an internal marking, and treats applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds.

Facilities access outside South Carolina is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Inside South Carolina, restroom access is now governed by House Bill 4756, signed by Governor Henry McMaster on Friday 15 May 2026. The law requires transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth, extending the pre-existing restriction to university campuses. The ACLU of South Carolina, responding on 18 May 2026, framed the measure as discrimination against trans students in both K-12 and higher education, and noted that the Senate amended the bill before passage.

A July 2026 national risk assessment ranks states by the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills. It records South Carolina's expansion of the bathroom ban to universities and places the state among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier. Federal custody and care policy sits above all of this: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025, and in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," the Department of Justice subpoenaed records from over 20 hospitals in summer 2025, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
South Carolina's 2026 expansion fits a national pattern rather than standing apart from it. The July 2026 assessment that ranks states by bill severity places South Carolina among the escalating states, a tier below the harshest. Facility restrictions have spread far beyond legislatures that acted first: nine states and one territory apply bathroom bans to K-12 schools and some government buildings, and additional states impose outright bans on facility use per gender identity.

Other jurisdictions have moved faster and further. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Enforcement precedent exists elsewhere. The April 2025 arrest of a transgender student in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol shows that restroom statutes of the kind South Carolina has adopted can produce custodial outcomes, not merely administrative refusal.
localsOnly:
South Carolina operates a "freeze-frame" policy restricting the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. The policy governs in-prison treatment only; it is not a housing-placement rule, and it does not by itself determine cell assignment, special-unit placement, or segregation. Metro Weekly reported on 11 July 2026 that the Transitics tracker places South Carolina among four states holding such freeze-frame policies, alongside Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah.

House Bill 4756 binds residents who study or work in the state's public education system. The ACLU of South Carolina stated in its 18 May 2026 response that the measure reaches students in K-12 schools as well as colleges and universities, and that the Senate amended the bill before passage, so the enacted text differs from the version first introduced.
outOfScopeNotes:
No South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, or solitary or segregation for trans prisoners is recorded in the available material. Whether courts in the state have addressed those questions remains unresolved rather than settled either way.

The available sources do not state when House Bill 4756 takes effect, what penalties attach to a restroom violation, or whether the requirement reaches private colleges and universities. These points are not sourced and would need verification against the enacted text.

The July 2026 assessment's tier placement rests on its reading of bills rather than on documented enforcement, so the frequency of restroom complaints, investigations or disciplinary action under the South Carolina law is unverified.
